title: The bhog of a sehaj path
word: The bhog of a sehaj path
hookLine: some people slow down on a long book's last page; the Granth's last page sets out a platter
tomorrow: where would a whole Granth live in an ordinary house?

lines: SLOWING DOWN ON THE LAST CHAPTER.
cards: Some readers slow down on the last chapter of a long book, because they don't want it to be over. A few skip the last chapter entirely, just to keep the story going.
So, yesterday's question: what happens on the Granth's last page? Near the very end sits a short salok of Guru Arjan's called the Mundavani, the seal. And it doesn't read like an ending.
It reads like a table being set.

teach.b: Guru Arjan writes, in paraphrase: on this platter three things have been placed, truth, contentment and contemplation, and the nectar of the Name, the support of all. Whoever eats it and enjoys it is carried across.
Notice where that leaves a reader after years of pages: not at a wall, at a meal. So the last page of the long reading hands the reader a full plate. That's the bhog, the completion of a sehaj path.
Some include the Raagmala that follows; others don't, and the Sikh code leaves that to the custom of the place, with no quarrel over it.
Then comes the Anand, Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, the same hymn that opened with finding the Guru with ease. Then the Ardas, the standing prayer.
Then karah prashad, warm and sweet, shared by everyone in the room.
Something to tell someone tonight: a reading that may take years ends with a plate of three things and a bowl of something sweet. The finish isn't a sigh. It's joy.

how: At the bhog of a sehaj path, the final pages of the Guru Granth Sahib are read (with or without the Raagmala, by local custom), followed by the Anand Sahib, the Ardas and the sharing of karah prashad, often with family and friends gathered.

games.q: what does “the bhog of a sehaj path” mean?
o: a fast kept until a reading is finished
the first page read when a reading starts
the joyful completion of a full reading

games.q: finish with joy — tap the pairs.
p: the completion of a full reading
read or not, by the custom of the place

s: a sehaj path ends in solemn silence
it ends with the Anand, a song of bliss, the Ardas, and sweet karah prashad shared.
near the Granth's end, the Mundavani pictures a platter of truth, contentment and contemplation
and the nectar of the Name, the support of all.
every gurdwara must read the Raagmala at the close
the Sikh code leaves it to the custom of the place, with no quarrel over it.

games.q: two aunts planning a bhog disagree about reading the Raagmala at the end, and it's getting tense. what does the Sikh code say?
o: it must always be read, or the reading isn't complete.
it must never be read; the reading ends at the Mundavani.
follow the custom of the place, and don't let it become a quarrel.
games.why: the code lets a reading close with the Mundavani or the Raagmala by local custom, and asks that the difference not become a fight. finish with joy.

practice: Count on your fingers the people you'd want in the room at the end of something long you're working on, one finger for each. For each one, give a quiet thank-you for a way they've helped you keep going.
Then breathe, and let the last finger rest in your palm like something sweet you're about to share.

wordCard.voice: The bhog of a sehaj path: the completion of a full reading, with the last pages, the Anand, the Ardas and karah prashad shared. The sixteenth word of the year.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhog, the completion of a reading of the Granth.

carryVoice: Your line: finish with joy. The last page sets a table, and everyone gets a plate. Two weeks of the page, closed.
